slides.title: Your fingers have zero muscles
slides.body: Every finger movement is pulled by muscles in your palm and forearm, through long tendons.
slides.image_prompt: Anatomical model of a human hand skeleton with thin white cords running from the fingertip bones down toward the wrist, soft studio light, dark background

slides.title: Puppet strings
slides.body: Tendons run like strings from forearm muscles to your fingertips. Wiggle your fingers and watch your forearm move.
slides.image_prompt: Wooden marionette hand hanging from taut strings attached to a wooden control bar, warm light, dark minimal background
slides.credit: Foto:Karl Heinz Hernried. (Public domain) via wikimedia

slides.title: The ring finger trap
slides.body: Fold your middle finger under, fingertips flat on a table. Your ring finger barely lifts: it shares tendons with its neighbors.
slides.image_prompt: Wooden artist mannequin hand resting flat on a wooden table, middle finger folded under, soft side lighting, shallow depth of field

slides.title: 9 tendons, one tunnel
slides.body: Nine finger tendons and a nerve squeeze through one narrow wrist channel. Swelling there causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
slides.image_prompt: Nine glowing threads and one yellow cord passing through a narrow stone archway shaped like a wrist bone, dramatic light, dark background

caption:
Your fingers have no muscles inside them. Every grip, tap and typed word is powered by muscles in your palm and forearm that pull on long tendons, like strings on a puppet.

That is why your forearm moves when you wiggle your fingers, and why one swollen spot in your wrist, the carpal tunnel, can numb your whole hand. Follow for one body fact your brain won't believe, every day.

Did you try the ring finger trick? Could you lift it?
